title: Heritage, folk music and cultural borrowing
summary: Everyone should embrace his own heritage; folk music becomes a museum piece.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: They were; I remember that period of time, very well. But I think the critics had been pushing this sort of thing for at least twenty years before that. John Hammond certainly is one, and I'm not negating John's purposes; I think they're fine. This is now why I'm talking like this, not at all.

I'm well aware of the debts we owe other people, but I also tend, for one reason, why should I deny my own heritage or you yours; you shouldn't, it's wrong to do that. You become something of a dilettante
if you don't do that, because how could you be something you are not.
I see a lot of kids trying to do it with India today; it doesn't work either.
The best Indian musicians spend a lifetime.

That gets into the folk era, the folk idiom, and this is really basically part of the argument before too. It's so strange, you think about these things all the time, and you put them into words and they sound empty.

But culturally, what gave rise to the folk music is the necessity from the environment, the way people were living. It forced it to grow the way it did. Time and events took away its raison d'etre. It becomes historical, it becomes a museum piece at one point, especially when you go in to record it.
